title: WHY DID JESUS CALL JUDAS “FRIEND” WHILE JUDAS WAS BETRAYING HIM?
paragraphs: WHY DID JESUS CALL JUDAS “FRIEND” WHILE JUDAS WAS BETRAYING HIM?
The Last Word Jesus Gave His Betrayer May Be One of the Most Terrifying—and Beautiful—Words in the Gospel
The kiss had barely left His face.
Torches burned through the darkness.
Weapons glimmered between the olive trees.
Boots moved through Gethsemane.
The disciples were confused. Fear was spreading. Violence was seconds away.
And standing directly in front of Jesus was a man who had eaten at His table.
Walked beside Him.
Listened to Him preach.
Watched Him heal the sick.
Saw demons flee.
Saw storms obey.
Saw the dead raised.
Had his feet washed by Him.
And now Judas had brought armed men to arrest Him.
Thirty pieces of silver had purchased the betrayal.
A kiss identified the victim.
And then Jesus spoke.
But He did not say, “Traitor.”
He did not say, “Monster.”
He did not say, “Enemy.”
Matthew records something far more unsettling:
“Friend.”
Read that again.
Friend.
Why?
Why would Jesus call Judas “friend” at the very moment Judas was betraying Him?
And perhaps the more uncomfortable question is not what that word tells us about Judas.
Perhaps it is what that word reveals about Jesus.
Because buried inside this brief exchange is something about the heart of Christ that becomes almost unbearable when you realize how personally it applies to us.
The Greek text of Matthew 26:50 reads:
ὁ δὲ Ἰησοῦς εἶπεν αὐτῷ· Ἑταῖρε, ἐφ’ ὃ πάρει.
Ho de Iēsous eipen autō: Hetaire, eph’ ho parei.
The key word is:
Ἑταῖρε — Hetaire.
It is commonly translated “Friend.”
But we need to be careful here.

Matthew did not use the ordinary Greek word we might expect for a deeply beloved, intimate friend. The word hetairos can carry the sense of companion, associate, comrade, or someone connected with another.
That matters.
In Matthew’s Gospel, this form of the word appears only three times: Matthew 20:13, Matthew 22:12, and here in Matthew 26:50.
And each setting carries weight.
This is not Jesus pretending that Judas’s betrayal does not matter.
It is not sentimental approval.
It is certainly not Jesus saying, “What you are doing is acceptable.”
Jesus never confused love with approval of evil.
Grace does not call darkness light.
Mercy does not redefine sin.
The same Christ who welcomed sinners also commanded repentance.
So when Jesus says, “Ἑταῖρε,” we are witnessing something much deeper than casual friendliness.
Judas is being confronted by the One he has betrayed—and Jesus still speaks without hatred.
Think about that.
Jesus knows everything.
He knows about the money.
He knows about the arrangement.
He knows why the soldiers are there.
He knows what the kiss means.
He knows what is coming next.
The beating.
The mockery.
The false accusations.
The scourging.
The nails.
The cross.
And He knows that Judas has chosen to participate in the chain of events leading there.
Yet Jesus does not become sinful in response to Judas’s sin.
That may be one of the most overlooked displays of Christ’s holiness in Gethsemane.
Judas can betray Jesus.
But Judas cannot make Jesus become like Judas.
Human beings often work differently.
Someone wounds us, and suddenly we believe their sin gives us permission to sin.
They lie about us, so we destroy their reputation.
They abandon us, so we become bitter.
They humiliate us, so we fantasize about humiliating them.
They betray us, so we allow hatred to occupy rooms in our hearts where Christ should reign.
We tell ourselves:
“They deserve it.”
Maybe they do deserve judgment.
But so did we.
That is where Gethsemane begins turning the mirror toward us.
Because it is comfortable to stand beside Jesus and stare at Judas.
It is much harder to realize how often we have resembled him.
No, perhaps you never sold Jesus for thirty pieces of silver.
But have you ever traded obedience for something cheaper?
Approval?
Pleasure?
Money?
Pornography?
Status?
A relationship you knew was pulling you away from God?
Secret sin?
Pride?
Bitterness?
The need to be admired?
The desperate hunger to belong?
How many times have our lips worshiped Jesus while our choices betrayed Him?
Judas betrayed Christ with a kiss.
And there is something terrifying about that.
Because the kiss looked like affection.
That means outward closeness to Jesus is not necessarily inward surrender to Jesus.
You can know Christian language and still have an unsurrendered heart.
You can sing worship songs and hide sin.
You can quote Scripture and resist Scripture.
You can attend church and never truly bow before the King.
You can call Him “Lord” with your mouth while quietly negotiating the price at which you will disobey Him.
That is why Judas should never merely become the villain in someone else’s story.
Judas is a warning.
Especially to religious people.
Especially to people who have been around Jesus long enough to become familiar with holy things.
Judas had extraordinary proximity to Christ.
But proximity is not the same thing as transformation.
He heard sermons from the greatest Preacher who ever lived.
Still he betrayed Him.
He witnessed miracles from the hands of God incarnate.
Still he betrayed Him.
He traveled with Jesus.
Still he betrayed Him.
He was trusted with responsibility among the Twelve.
Still he betrayed Him.
The problem was never insufficient exposure to Jesus.
Something in Judas remained unsurrendered.
And that should make every one of us ask a question that hurts:
What have I kept from Jesus?
Not what does everybody know about.
What have I kept hidden?
What private compromise have I learned to manage?
What resentment have I renamed “discernment”?
What greed have I renamed “ambition”?
What lust have I renamed “weakness”?
What disobedience have I renamed “my personal choice”?
What unforgiveness have I justified because the wound was real?
Be honest.
This may be hitting harder than you expected.
And if it is, do not run.
Conviction is not the same thing as condemnation.
The Gospel does not expose our darkness so that we can admire how dark it is.
Jesus brings darkness into the light because He came to save sinners.
That is why the word in Gethsemane matters.
Ἑταῖρε.
Friend.
There is restraint in it.
There is confrontation in it.
There is tragedy in it.
There is history behind it.
Judas is standing before the Man whose bread he ate, whose roads he walked, whose voice he heard, whose miracles he witnessed.
Jesus knows exactly who is standing before Him.
And Jesus does not answer betrayal with hatred.
But notice something else.
Jesus also does not chase Judas with cheap grace.
He does not pretend nothing happened.
Luke preserves another piercing part of the encounter:
“Judas, would you betray the Son of Man with a kiss?”
Imagine hearing your own name from Jesus while committing the sin you thought you had already decided to commit.
“Judas…”
There are moments when God’s truth reaches us while our hand is still touching the forbidden thing.
While the message is still being typed.
While the affair is still secret.
While the bottle is still hidden.
While the bitterness is still being rehearsed.
While the compromise is still being justified.
While everyone else thinks we are fine.
And somewhere beneath all the noise, the Word of God touches the conscience.
You know.
You know this is not who Christ is calling you to be.
That moment is mercy.
Do not confuse mercy with permission.
God's patience with sin is not God's approval of sin.
Sometimes the fact that judgment has not yet fallen is itself an invitation to repent.
And Judas’s story becomes especially painful because another disciple also failed Jesus that night.
Peter.
Peter did not sell Jesus.
But Peter denied knowing Him.
Not once.
Three times.
Peter had boasted that he would remain faithful.
Then fear entered the courtyard.
And courage disappeared.
“I do not know the man.”
Imagine those words.
The disciple who once confessed Jesus as the Christ now denies even knowing Him.
Judas failed Jesus.
Peter failed Jesus.
Yet their stories did not end the same way.
Why?
Not because Peter’s sin was harmless.
It was not.
Not because Peter deserved restoration.
He did not.
The difference becomes visible in what happened afterward.
Peter was broken and eventually restored to Christ.
Judas was filled with remorse, but his story descended into despair and death.
This distinction matters enormously.
There is a kind of sorrow that merely hates the consequences of sin.
And there is godly sorrow that turns toward God.
The Gospel does not say, “Feel terrible enough and perhaps God will forgive you.”
The Gospel says something infinitely better.
Turn to Christ.
Come into the light.
Confess.
Repent.
Trust the Savior who died for sinners.
Because your hope has never been the quality of your past.
Your hope is Jesus.
And here is where Gethsemane becomes almost overwhelming.
The soldiers think they are taking Jesus.
Judas thinks he has delivered Jesus.
The religious authorities think their plan is succeeding.
But Jesus is not accidentally stumbling toward Calvary.
He is giving Himself.
The betrayal is evil.
The conspiracy is evil.
The false accusations are evil.
The cruelty is evil.
Human beings remain morally responsible for what they do.
Yet none of it overturns the redemptive purpose of God.
Jesus goes toward the cross willingly.
And at that cross, something astonishing happens.
The sinless One bears the judgment sinners deserve.
The Betrayed One dies for betrayers.
The Denied One dies for deniers.
The Rejected One dies for rebels.
The Holy One dies for the unholy.
The King wears thorns.
The Creator is pierced by creatures.
The Son of God enters death.
And three days later, death discovers that it has swallowed Someone it cannot hold.
Jesus Christ rises.
That is Christianity.
Not “become good enough so God might tolerate you.”
Not “hide your scandal so religious people will respect you.”
Not “repair yourself and then approach Jesus.”
No.
Christ came for sinners.
Repentance means we stop defending our rebellion and turn toward Him.
Grace means forgiveness cannot be purchased by our goodness.
The cross means our sin is more serious than we wanted to admit.
The resurrection means Christ is more powerful than we dared to hope.
This is why Judas’s kiss should disturb us.
And this is why Jesus’s response should break us.
Because some people reading this have spent years believing:
“If people knew what I did, they would never look at me the same.”
Maybe they would not.
Jesus already knows.
Others are thinking:
“I have gone too far.”
Others:
“I knew better.”
Others:
“I promised God I would stop.”
Others:
“I failed again.”
Others:
“I still believe in Jesus, but I barely recognize myself anymore.”
Listen carefully.
Do not turn Judas into an excuse for despair.
Let his story become a warning that drives you toward Christ.
Peter fell terribly.
But failure did not get the final word.
Jesus did.
And that is the Gospel Warrior message:
Not because scandal is imaginary.
Not because consequences disappear.
Not because repentance is optional.
Jesus rewrites everything because the crucified and risen Christ can redeem people whose stories look irredeemable.
He can forgive the guilty.
Restore the fallen.
Cleanse the ashamed.
Break chains.
Expose idols.
Heal wounded hearts.
Teach bitter people to forgive.
Call wandering sons and daughters home.
And make new creations out of people who thought their worst chapter had already become their final chapter.
Maybe this article was never primarily about Judas.
Maybe God allowed you to read this far because there is something in your own heart you have been avoiding.
Something hidden.
Something defended.
Something exhausting you.
You do not need another mask.
You need Jesus.
Not merely Christianity as a label.
Not merely inspirational content.
Not merely religious habits.
Christ Himself.
Not because strangers need the details of your sin.
They do not.
But sometimes a simple confession that you need Christ becomes the first crack in the wall you have spent years building.
And if Christ has already carried you through a season you thought would destroy you, tell someone what He has done.
Your testimony may become the sentence another wounded person desperately needs tonight.
There may be a prodigal pretending everything is fine.
There may be someone quietly wondering whether Jesus could still receive them.
There may even be someone who does not yet believe the Gospel at all.
There may come a night when betrayal hurts differently.
When your own failure feels heavier.
When someone else's sin makes hatred feel justified.
Come back to Gethsemane.
Come back to that word.
Ἑταῖρε.
Remember the Savior who could stand before His betrayer without becoming corrupted by betrayal.
Remember the Savior who went from that garden toward a cross.
Remember the Savior who rose.
And remember that following Jesus means more than consuming Christian content.
It means becoming His disciple.
Invite your family.
Invite the friend drifting from God.
Invite the believer who is tired.
Invite the seeker with difficult questions.
Invite the lukewarm Christian who needs awakening.
Invite even the unbeliever who thinks Christianity has nothing meaningful to say to broken people.
I want to say this carefully because Scripture matters too much to manipulate.
And your sharing matters too.
A Facebook share helps carry the message.
Both can become acts of willing stewardship when they are done freely, prayerfully, and for the glory of God.
It is Scripture.
It is becoming harder to deceive because you know the Word.
It is becoming quicker to repent because you love Christ more than your excuses.
It is feeding your soul something deeper than another endless scroll.
And comment—not for an algorithm alone, but because faith was never meant to be lived behind a mask.
“Christ is still healing me.”
Five words.
Maybe that is your testimony tonight.
And before you leave, look once more into Gethsemane.
See the torches.
Hear the footsteps.
See Judas approaching.
Watch the kiss.
Then listen.
Jesus knows.
Jesus sees.
Jesus is not deceived.
And still Christ walks toward the cross.
Not because betrayal wins.
Because redemption is coming.
That is the part darkness never understands.
The enemy can wound the story.
Sin can scar the story.
People can betray the story.
You can even make terrible decisions inside your own story.
But when a sinner truly turns to Jesus Christ in repentance and faith, the worst chapter does not have authority to write the ending.
The kiss of betrayal was not the final word—the empty tomb was.
